summary:
We developed a story-driven, 2D educational game in Unity that turns space mission design into an interactive adventure. Players become a scientist with fragmented memories, solving puzzles to uncover their past and prepare for a mission to locate and safely recover a vaccine. Along the way, they apply physics concepts, manage limited resources, and choose scientific instruments within strict mass and power budgets.

Our project addresses the challenge by connecting scientific objectives, engineering requirements, and operational constraints through gameplay. Rather than presenting mission design as isolated calculations, it allows players to explore how individual decisions affect the mission as a whole. Equipment must be selected not just for its capabilities, but for its contribution to the mission within available resources.

By combining exploration, storytelling, and hands-on problem-solving, the game makes complex concepts more approachable for students and aspiring engineers. It encourages curiosity and systems thinking while demonstrating a central lesson of space exploration: successful missions depend on balancing ambitious goals with practical limitations.
details:
What We Developed

We developed a story-driven, 2D educational game in Unity that introduces players to space mission design through exploration, puzzles, and resource-management decisions. Players take on the role of a scientist with fragmented memories who must recover knowledge and prepare for a mission to locate and safely retrieve a vaccine.

The game connects its story to its learning objectives: as players solve problems, they uncover pieces of the scientist’s past and learn concepts needed for the mission. Our prototype focuses on physics-based reasoning, managing limited resources, and selecting scientific instruments rather than attempting to reproduce every aspect of a professional mission simulator.

How the Game Works

Players explore the environment and interact with designated stations to open puzzle interfaces. These interactions turn mission preparation into practical tasks, requiring players to interpret clues, adjust values, and make decisions.

One puzzle features two adjustable levers representing mass and velocity. Players must find a combination whose product reaches a target value within the permitted limits. Instead of simply reading an equation, they manipulate its variables and explore how different combinations can satisfy the same requirement.

Another puzzle challenges players to choose from seven instruments and pieces of equipment, each with a purpose, mass, and power requirement. With a remaining mass allowance of 25 kilograms and a limited power budget, they cannot take everything. Their selection must provide the capabilities needed to assess environmental conditions, navigate and locate the vaccine, and recover and preserve it safely.

Dialogue describes the mission’s needs without directly naming the correct equipment. Players must connect those needs to the available tools. This makes success depend on understanding what an instrument contributes—not merely choosing items that fit within a numerical limit.

Together, these challenges demonstrate that a mission’s objective, equipment, and available resources must be considered as a connected system.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our goal is to make space mission design more approachable for students, aspiring engineers, and curious players. The game provides an environment where they can experiment with decisions and practice scientific reasoning without needing access to spacecraft hardware or specialist engineering software.

The learning experience emphasizes problem-solving rather than memorization. Players must identify requirements, compare options, recognize constraints, and revise their choices. A piece of equipment may be useful, but that does not automatically make it suitable for the mission when its mass and power demands are considered.

Our intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space exploration and develop systems thinking: understanding how one decision affects other parts of a mission. The game could support classroom discussions or informal learning activities by giving players a shared experience of making engineering trade-offs.

Tools and Development

We used Unity as the game engine and C# as the programming language to develop character movement, interaction triggers, puzzle logic, equipment-selection rules, and progression conditions.

The visual experience uses 2D environment artwork, character sprites, and animation. Interactive puzzle panels provide controls such as sliders and equipment selections, while keyboard-based exploration connects these interfaces to the game world.

We also developed automated model tests to check puzzle logic and produced a Linux desktop build. The project is a software-based prototype using keyboard and mouse input; it does not rely on custom physical hardware.

What Makes the Project Creative

The project combines a memory-recovery mystery with engineering education. The scientist’s recovery of knowledge mirrors the player’s learning journey, giving scientific concepts a purpose within the story.

Rather than interrupting gameplay with unrelated quizzes, we make learning part of the action. Players operate machines, interpret mission clues, and assemble an equipment set to accomplish a meaningful objective. The vaccine-recovery mission provides a concrete reason to consider environmental assessment, navigation, and preservation together.

This approach makes mission preparation both a narrative experience and a sequence of connected scientific decisions.

Factors We Considered

We balanced scientific clarity with approachable gameplay. The puzzles use simplified relationships and explicit constraints so players can understand the underlying ideas without being overwhelmed by the complexity of a real mission.

We also considered the balance between guidance and discovery. Dialogue provides enough context to support reasoning while leaving players responsible for identifying the solution. Mass and power limits prevent “take everything” strategies, and equipment requirements ensure that meeting the budget alone is not enough.

Finally, we focused the prototype on a manageable set of connected mechanics. Our central design principle is that a successful mission is not about choosing the most powerful equipment—it is about choosing the right combination of capabilities within the resources available.
